answer:
Overall, Tremorlog is a promising but early-stage concept with a real, well-articulated problem and a pragmatic solution, though its differentiation and defensibility are not yet proven.

Strengths: (1) The pain point is genuine and clearly identified. Infrequent, short neurology visits (every 3-6 months) yield only a snapshot of a fluctuating condition, patient recall is unreliable (especially with cognitive effects), and paper diaries are subjective. The comparison to continuous home monitoring in diabetes is apt. (2) The idea is grounded in lived observation: Priyanka saw the information gap firsthand while volunteering at a movement disorders clinic, which lends credibility to the problem framing. (3) The solution is well matched to the user. A web app with no download, a two-minute daily routine, and use of a camera patients already own lowers adoption friction for an older population and keeps deployment cost low versus hardware-based competitors. (4) Serving both sides (patient trend view and clinician dashboard with flagged changes and reviewable clips) creates a coherent workflow value proposition, and selling to small and mid-sized clinics is a sensible entry point. (5) Early traction is meaningful for a student team: a working prototype and a paying pilot client suggest at least one buyer sees enough value to pay.

Weaknesses and risks: (1) Uniqueness is moderate rather than compelling. Wearable sensors, FDA-cleared wrist devices, telehealth platforms, and diary apps already address parts of the problem. The only stated advantage is no hardware and lower cost, which is a convenience and cost advantage, not a defensible moat. Camera-based tremor analysis is also technically replicable. (2) The core value claim is unvalidated. The team openly admits video-based scores are likely less accurate than dedicated sensors and have not been benchmarked against clinical rating scales (e.g., MDS-UPDRS). If clinicians do not trust the score, the product's value collapses; this is the central make-or-break question. (3) Scope is narrow. Tremor is only one Parkinson's symptom (bradykinesia, rigidity, gait, and medication on/off states matter clinically), so the product may be seen as a feature rather than a complete monitoring solution. (4) Compliance and regulatory risk are underdeveloped: patient video is sensitive health data, there is no clarity on HIPAA obligations, whether the software constitutes a regulated medical device (FDA), or which reimbursement codes apply. The business model's justification rests partly on unconfirmed reimbursement. (5) Adherence and clinical workflow questions are unaddressed: will patients actually record daily, and will busy clinicians review dashboards and act on the data? Alert fatigue and added workload are real adoption barriers. (6) Team and market sizing gaps: no physician or regulatory expertise on the team, no bottom-up market sizing, an unformed legal entity, and projections (about $50K ARR from 10 clinics/200 patients) built on largely untested assumptions.

Conclusion: The need is real and the solution is thoughtfully tailored to it, giving the idea solid conceptual merit and a credible early signal via the paid pilot. However, the offering is not yet unique or compelling enough to stand out against established alternatives, and its viability hinges on clinical validation, regulatory clarity, and proof of sustained patient and clinician engagement. The funding request is appropriately targeted at exactly these gaps, which reflects good self-awareness. I would rate the concept as good with meaningful upside, but still high risk until validation data and regulatory/reimbursement pathways are established.
